newsitem.title: GREECE: GREENPEACE HAILS REFINERY PROTEST AS SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: GREENPEACE HAILS REFINERY PROTEST AS SUCCESS.

text.p: Greenpeace on Thursday declared its blockade of Greece's largest refinery a success for creating a wave of strong reaction against oil pollution from political parties and the public.
A Greek prosecutor charged 17 Greenpeace protestors for staging the blockade at the Motor Oil refinery near the Corinth canal on Wendesday. They were arrested after a raid by coast guard commandos.
It is the first time Greece has brought criminal charges against the international environmental group. The defendants include people from Britain, Austria and Germany.
The military-type operation prompted heated reaction from several Greek political parties and the media while local residents rallied to support the defendants.
"Our political target was achieved because we revealed the real face of Motor Oil and the oil industry. They don't care about the environment," Greenpeace activist Stelios Psomas said.
He said the socialist government had ignored Greenpeace's demands to make stricter oil pollution laws.
"We are more than pleased with the public support we got and I have a feeling we stirred up thousands who never dared to speak up against Motor Oil and Vardinoyannis," he said.

Motor Oil, which has an annual capacity of five million tonnes is jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Greek Vardinoyannis family. It employs about 1,300 people and had a 1994 turnover of about $750 million.
The company defended its environmental record, saying it took more precautions than required by Greek law.
Greenpeace activists chained themselves to mooring buoys and loading cranes at its port facilities early on Tuesday, blocking access for 24 hours.
Their violent removal by coast guard commandos wearing hoods and carrying machine guns prompted strong press reaction.
"This kind of reaction embarrasses our country internationally," a commentator said on popular Flash radio.
Three opposition parties condemned the operation and Merchant Marine Minister Stavros Soumakis offered an apology.
"I am honestly sorry if my orders to remove the activists peacefully were not followed and special forces were used," he told reporters.
The Left Coalition party brought the issue to parliament, where the Environment Ministry must formally respond next week to questions about its oil pollution record.

"We asked the government, instead of arrests and violence against environmental groups, to explain its refusal to push tough safety rules and adopt Greenpeace's proposals on oil pollution," the party said in a statement.
The activists were charged with trespassing and hindering a public service company and were set free after the trial was set for February 6. They face up to five years in jail if convicted.
Scores of local residents gathered outside the prosecutors office to cheer the activists, shouting slogans such as "Hands off Greenpeace". --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
